metric.why: PPAs are how the boom finances new generation and how operators back renewable claims. Nuclear agreements, including restarts and small modular commitments, became the signature deals of the AI era.
metric.definition: Long-term contracts by which operators secure generation, nuclear, solar, wind, or gas, for current and future facilities.

reading.body:
Power purchase agreements are the financial instrument that converts AI demand into new generation capacity, making them the clearest link between data center construction and the grid's ability to keep pace.

When an operator signs a long-term PPA, it commits future revenue to a generator, which then has the collateral to finance construction or restart. Without that contract, merchant generation carries too much risk to build speculatively. Nuclear agreements, including restarts and small modular reactor commitments, became prominent precisely because AI operators need firm, around-the-clock power that solar and wind alone cannot guarantee. The PPA is therefore not just a procurement tool but a signal to capital markets that load is real and durable.

The data identifies PPAs as a market-tracking metric within the broader power and grid category, alongside interconnection queue position, approval to energize, capacity market clearing prices, and behind-the-meter generation. That placement matters: a signed PPA does not mean power flows. An operator can hold a contract and still sit in an interconnection queue for years, waiting for grid approval. The PPA secures the generation side of the equation; the companion metrics track whether that power can actually reach the facility.

What this data does not cover is the volume, geography, or terms of any specific agreement. It establishes what PPAs are and why they matter structurally, but readers looking for contract counts, prices, or counterparties will need sources beyond this metric's definition.
